Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Andes Virus Exposure and Nosocomial Transmission Events to Healthcare Personnel: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) is a high-consequence infectious disease with substantial mortality. On 2 May 2026, the World Health Organization reported a multinational ANDV outbreak, raising questions regarding the risk of transmission to healthcare personnel (HCP). METHODS: We performed a systematic review per PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO:CRD420261283806) for studies describing healthcare-associated ANDV exposure or transmission events to HCP. RESULTS: Eight studies reporting on 7 events were included, describing a total of 17 healthcare-associated cases. Overall, 207 individuals were exposed, including 118 HCP, resulting in 8 infections and 4 deaths among HCP. Studies describing HCP infections reported none or inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. CONCLUSIONS: Transmission of ANDV to HCP has been reported in the setting of delayed implementation of transmission-based precautions or breaches in infection control practice. Limitations in published exposure events highlight the need for standardized reporting of exposure events and outcomes as well as infection prevention measures implemented.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

papers.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 6 조회 1 다운로드 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.

full_text_sections.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 6 조회 1 다운로드 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.

analysis.background: The paper addresses the problem of identifying the causative agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever (EHF), a critical step for disease control, and argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus resulted from repeated failures and trials.
analysis.methods: Lee’s work from 1970‑1980 progressed through three phases: initially using wild rats as experimental objects (1970‑1973) without success; then introducing lung tissue of wild rats and applying the Fluorescent Antibody Technique to identify the Korea Antigen (1974‑1976); and finally characterizing its physicochemical properties (1977‑1980).
analysis.results: The Korea Antigen was identified as the EHF agent using the new tissue source and antibody technique, its physicochemical features were clarified, and in 1980 the antigen was officially registered as Hantaan virus.
analysis.contribution: The study highlights the historical scientific process leading to the discovery and formal registration of Hantaan virus, illustrating the importance of trial‑and‑error experimentation in virology.
analysis.limitations: The article provides only a historical narrative based on abstract and partial text, lacking primary experimental data or detailed quantitative results.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The paper examines the challenge of identifying the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus arose from repeated failures. Methods: Lee’s research from 1970‑1980 used wild rats, then lung tissue of wild rats with Fluorescent Antibody Technique, and later physicochemical analyses. Results: The Korea Antigen was identified as the EHF agent, its properties were clarified, and it was registered as Hantaan virus in 1980. Contribution: The work documents the historical trial‑and‑error process that led to the virus’s discovery and registration. Limitations: Only abstract and partial text are available, with no primary data reported.

papers.title_zh: Ho Wang Lee 对流行性出血热的研究及对 汉滩病毒 的发现

analysis_zh.background: 本文讨论了确定流行性出血热(EHF)致病因子的难题,这是疾病控制的关键步骤,并指出 Ho Wang Lee 对 汉滩病毒 的发现是通过反复失败和试验得来的。
analysis_zh.methods: Lee 在 1970‐1980 年的研究分为三个阶段:第一阶段(1970‐1973)使用野生大鼠作为实验对象,但未取得成功;第二阶段(1974‐1976)引入野生大鼠肺组织并采用荧光抗体技术鉴定 Korea 抗原;第三阶段(1977‐1980)对其理化特性进行表征。
analysis_zh.results: 利用新的组织来源和抗体技术,将 Korea 抗原确定为 EHF 病原体,阐明了其理化特性,并于 1980 年正式登记为 汉滩病毒。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究突出展示了导致 汉滩病毒 发现及正式登记的历史科学过程,说明了在病毒学中反复试验的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本文仅基于摘要和部分文本提供历史叙述,缺乏原始实验数据或详细的定量结果。

papers.title: Learning from COVID-19 to strengthen hantavirus preparedness and public health response
papers.abstract: Years after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the world continues to face significant health, social, and economic challenges, while emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases remain a growing global public health concern. This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. COVID-19 spreads efficiently between humans and caused a global pandemic, whereas Hantavirus infections are mainly transmitted from rodents to humans and remain geographically localized despite a higher case fatality rate. While vaccines are available for COVID-19, none exist for Hantavirus disease. The study also highlights the value of artificial intelligence, epidemic intelligence, and the One Health approach for improving outbreak prediction, detection, and surveillance.

This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. Keywords Artificial intelligence, COVID-19, Hantavirus, One health, Public health, Zoonotic disease ​1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases caused by both novel and known patho­ gens are increasingly recognized as a major global public health concern [1]. Zoonoses are infectious diseases that can be transmitted between animals and humans through direct or indirect contact. They are caused by a broad range of pathogens, including bac­ teria, viruses, parasites, fungi, rickettsia, chlamydia, mycoplasma, and other infectious agents. Some zoonotic pathogens have multiple animal reservoir hosts that contribute to their maintenance and transmission by supporting pathogen persistence, amplification, Page 2 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 and spillover to humans. Zoonotic infections are estimated to cause approximately 2.7 million deaths each year, underscoring their substantial impact on global health [2, 3]. Environmental modifications, including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, agri­ cultural expansion, irrigation, urbanization, and climate change disrupt ecosystems and increase contact between humans and wildlife, and have given birth to zoonotic diseases, such as malaria and Lyme disease, thereby facilitating pathogen spillover. Changes in the abundance and distribution of animal hosts can strongly influence the occurrence and transmission of zoonotic diseases in humans. For example, El Niño events in 1991–1992 and 1997–1998 in the southwestern United States (U.S) increased precipitation and veg­ etation growth, providing more food for rodents and resulting in a substantial increase in rodent populations. This ecological cascade favored hantavirus transmission among rodents and subsequently contributed to an increase in human hantavirus cases [3]. At the same time, population growth and the increasing demand for food have increased human exposure to food-borne zoonotic pathogens. Although wildlife contributes less to global food consumption than domestic livestock, the trade and consumption of wild­ life can increase opportunities for pathogens to cross species barriers. For instance, in Europe, changes in vegetation, food availability, water resources, climate, and land use can increase rodent populations and human exposure [4]. In Argentina, climate change and habitat fragmentation have been linked to recent increases in cases by favoring rodent reservoirs [5], either directly (via winter survival) or indirectly (through food lim­ itation). Studies have also shown a positive association between bank vole density and PUUV prevalence [6]. Similarly, in Brazil and the western U.S, Hantavirus occurrence has been associated with socioeconomic factors, environmental conditions, and rodent diversity [7]. Due to environment disruption, several zoonotic diseases have demon­ strated their potential to cause severe outbreaks and widespread public health impacts, including hantavirus infections, Mpox, Ebola virus disease, and Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) [2, 3]. COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, provides a major example of a zoonotic disease with global health consequences. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, where early investigations suggested an epidemiological association between the initial cases and seafood and live-animal markets. Bats are considered a likely natural reservoir of related coronaviruses, while the potential role of other animals, including pangolins, as intermediate hosts remains uncertain and continues to be investigated [8, 9]. The COVID-19 pandemic placed zoonotic diseases at the forefront of global atten­ tion, demonstrating how disruptions at the human–animal–environment interface can have profound health, social, and economic consequences [3]. It underscored the impor­ tance of understanding these interconnected systems and exposed both the strengths and limitations of global public health preparedness and response capacities [10]. Recently, the world has experienced a new hantavirus outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV), associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius, which departed from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, 2026, and followed a South Atlantic itinerary before arriving in Cabo Verde [11, 12]. The outbreak was particularly significant not because it indicated pandemic-level transmissibility, but because it combined a severe zoonotic infection with delayed and nonspecific early symptoms, highly mobile international contacts, limited medical capacity aboard the ship, complex multijurisdictional oversight, and increased public Page 3 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 sensitivity to infectious disease outbreaks following the COVID-19 pandemic [13]. This raises an important question: how effective was the public health response to COVID- 19, and what lessons can be applied to the 2026 ANDV outbreak as a contemporary case study in a rapidly changing ecosystem? To address this question, this review adopts a comparative analysis by examining the epidemiological, virological, ecological, and public health dimensions of both diseases from an integrated multidisciplinary and environmental perspective. The literature search was initiated on 10 May 2026 and was continuously updated throughout the revision process to incorporate newly published and relevant evidence. Searches were conducted across major scientific databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, supplemented by information from authoritative public health agencies, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), using combinations of keywords related to “COVID-19”, “hanta­ virus”, “immunopathogenesis”, “diagnosis,” “surveillance” and “One Health”, along with additional search terms tailored to each specific subtopic. Ecological analyses and diag­ nostic evaluation studies were also considered. To minimize selection bias, study screen­ ing and eligibility assessment were performed independently by all the authors, with disagreements resolved through discussion. A predefined quality assessment was also applied to evaluate the methodological robustness and relevance of the included stud­ ies. Reference lists of relevant articles were also screened to identify additional studies. Sources were eligible for inclusion if they addressed one or more of these aspects and provided relevant evidence for understanding the similarities and differences between COVID-19 and hantavirus infections, as well as lessons for strengthening preparedness and public health responses to emerging zoonotic diseases. 2 Epidemiology In 2019, the new Coronavirus (CoV), SARS-CoV-2, has emerged, and rapidly spread globally. The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020 [8, 9]. The global COVID-19 numbers reported since the beginning of the pandemic until April 13, 2024 show a total of 704,753,890 cases, with 7,010,681 deaths and 675,619,811 recovered. After this date, the majority of countries have stopped reporting the COVID-19 statis­ tics. The peak reached 3,848,199 cases/daily on January 20, 2022 [14]. In Europe, the excess mortality rates ranged between 14.9% and 54.3% in 2020, with most of the deaths occurred in the eastern part of Europe. In May 2023, the excess mortality was reported to be 3.7% [15]. The mortality rate in America was 1% whereas the case fatality rates (CFRs) in Africa region were the lowest, ranging from 1.214% to 2.548% in 2022, and from 1.18% to 2.516% in 2024, as American and African countries were the last regions in the world to be affected by COVID-19. In Asia, the CFR ranged from 0.359% to 1.467% in 2022 and from 0.346% to 2.516% in 2024 [16–18]. SARS-CoV-2 was not the first CoV identified. CoVs are widespread viruses that infect both humans and animals, including birds and mammals, and are responsible for a substantial proportion of com­ mon cold cases. Before the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, six human coronaviruses were known: four typically caused mild respiratory illnesses, whereas two—SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV—were associated with severe and sometimes fatal disease [19]. Regarding the recent ANDV outbreak, a cluster of passengers presenting with severe respiratory illness aboard the vessel was reported to the WHO on 2 May 2026. The ship Page 4 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 was carrying 147 passengers and crew members. By 4 May 2026, seven hantavirus- related cases had been identified, including two laboratory-confirmed infections and five suspected cases. Among these cases, three deaths were reported, one patient was in critical condition, and three individuals presented with mild symptoms [11]. As of 2 July, a total of 13 cases had been reported, including three deaths, corresponding to a CFR of 23%. Twelve cases were laboratory-confirmed for ANDV infection, while one was classified as a probable case [20]. The reported cases included four Dutch, three British, two Spanish, one German, one Swiss, one French, and one Canadian national. Similar to CoVs, hantaviruses are not newly emerging pathogens; rather, they have long been recognized as important zoonotic viruses with established reservoirs and diverse trans­ mission patterns [21]. The infection appears to have been described in Chinese literature nearly 900 years ago, but gained global attention during the Korean War (1950–1953) [22, 23], when more than 3,000 United Nations soldiers developed hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Major outbreaks were also reported during World War II and the Balkan War, particularly among soldiers in Europe and Asia. The causative agent, Hantaan virus (HTNV), was identified in the early 1980s present in the lungs of its natural reservoir, the striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius). Overall, an estimated 10,000 to more than 100,000 Hantavirus infections occur worldwide each year, with the highest burden reported in Asia and Europe [24]. HFRS remains responsible for thou­ sands of annual cases, particularly in Asia and Europe, whereas hantavirus cardiopul­ monary syndrome (HCPS) occurs mainly in the Americas and is associated with higher mortality rates [22]. The CFR varies considerably by region, ranging from less than 1% to 15% in Asia and Europe and reaching up to 50% in the Americas [24]. Specifically, in Chile, nearly 70% of HCPS patients report occupational or peridomestic exposure to rodents or close contact with infected individuals, while 20–35% describe exposure dur­ ing recreational activities in high-risk areas [25, 26]. In Europe, 1,885 hantavirus cases were reported in 2023 (0.4 cases per 100,000 population), representing the lowest inci­ dence recorded between 2019 and 2023 [27]. In East Asia, HFRS continues to cause thousands of cases annually despite an overall declining trend [11]. In the United States (U.S), 890 hantavirus cases were reported between 1993 and 2023. In 2025, the Region of the Americas documented 229 cases and 59 deaths, corresponding to a CFR of 25.7%. In mainland France, hantavirus infection remains relatively rare, with between 14 and 320 confirmed HFRS cases reported annually since 2005, although the disease is more fre­ quent in Germany and Finland. In French Guiana, 13 confirmed hantavirus cases were identified between 2008 and May 2026 [26]. 3 Virology SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the family Coronaviridae and the order Nidovirales. It is an enveloped, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus composed of four major structural proteins: the envelope (E), membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), and spike (S) proteins [9]. SARS-CoV-2 is a zoonotic virus, with evidence supporting an animal origin and subse­ quent emergence in humans. Human-to-human transmission occurs primarily through close contact via respiratory droplets and aerosols released when an infected individual coughs, sneezes, speaks, sings, or breathes deeply, particularly in crowded or poorly ven­ tilated indoor environments. Transmission may also occur indirectly through contact with contaminated surfaces followed by touching the eyes, nose, or mouth before proper Page 5 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 hand hygiene [28]. The incubation period of SARS-CoV-2 generally ranges from 2 to 7 days [9]. Notably, SARS-CoV-2 is also capable of reverse zoonotic transmission, whereby humans can transmit the virus to animals, particularly mustelid species, tigers, lions, hyenas, as well as deer and hamsters [1, 29]. Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae within the order Bunyavirales [24]. They are enveloped, spherical RNA viruses and constitute a distinct genus within the former Bunyaviridae group. Their genome consists of three segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA sharing conserved 3′ terminal sequences. These segments include the small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, which encode the nucleoprotein (N), the envelope glycoproteins (Gn and Gc), and the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L protein), respectively [22]. Hantaviruses are primarily transmitted from rodents to humans [24]. However, unlike SARS-CoV-2, most hantaviruses are not transmitted from person to person. ANDV is the main hantavirus known to have this capacity, particu­ larly following close and prolonged contact with an infected individual. The first docu­ mented evidence of person-to-person transmission of ANDV was reported during an outbreak in Argentina in 1996 [30]. Subsequent cases of person-to-person transmission were reported in Argentina (1996 and 2018) and Chile (1997, 2004, and 2014), mainly in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly within households or dur­ ing the early prodromal phase of illness [31]. Moreover, the transmission of hantaviruses and spatiotemporal dynamics are influenced by a complex interplay of ecological factors, environmental conditions, and the behaviors of rodent reservoirs and human popula­ tions, all of which contribute to pathogen spread [4]. The incubation period of hantavi­ rus infection is generally longer than that of COVID-19 and generally ranges from 1 to 6 weeks following exposure [26]. In particular, the incubation period of ANDV ranges from 7 to 39 days, with a median of approximately 18 days, including among individuals with brief exposure periods of less than 48 h [25]. 4 Viral strains RNA viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses, have a high capacity for genetic variation and adaptation, allowing them to evolve rapidly, infect new hosts, and evade host immune responses. Their genetic diversity is driven mainly by mutation and, for some RNA viruses, by recombination, reassortment, and interactions among viral popu­ lations. These processes can generate new genetic variants and facilitate adaptation to changing host and environmental conditions [32]. For example, El Niño events in 1991–1992 and 1997–1998 in the southwestern United States (U.S) increased precipitation and veg­ etation growth, providing more food for rodents and resulting in a substantial increase in rodent populations. This ecological cascade favored hantavirus transmission among rodents and subsequently contributed to an increase in human hantavirus cases [3]. At the same time, population growth and the increasing demand for food have increased human exposure to food-borne zoonotic pathogens. Although wildlife contributes less to global food consumption than domestic livestock, the trade and consumption of wild­ life can increase opportunities for pathogens to cross species barriers. For instance, in Europe, changes in vegetation, food availability, water resources, climate, and land use can increase rodent populations and human exposure [4]. In Argentina, climate change and habitat fragmentation have been linked to recent increases in cases by favoring rodent reservoirs [5], either directly (via winter survival) or indirectly (through food lim­ itation). Studies have also shown a positive association between bank vole density and PUUV prevalence [6]. Similarly, in Brazil and the western U.S, Hantavirus occurrence has been associated with socioeconomic factors, environmental conditions, and rodent diversity [7]. Due to environment disruption, several zoonotic diseases have demon­ strated their potential to cause severe outbreaks and widespread public health impacts, including hantavirus infections, Mpox, Ebola virus disease, and Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) [2, 3]. COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, provides a major example of a zoonotic disease with global health consequences. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, where early investigations suggested an epidemiological association between the initial cases and seafood and live-animal markets. Bats are considered a likely natural reservoir of related coronaviruses, while the potential role of other animals, including pangolins, as intermediate hosts remains uncertain and continues to be investigated [8, 9]. The COVID-19 pandemic placed zoonotic diseases at the forefront of global atten­ tion, demonstrating how disruptions at the human–animal–environment interface can have profound health, social, and economic consequences [3]. papers.title: Hantavirus at the Climate–Rodent–Human Interface: Integrating Immunopathogenesis, Ecological Drivers, and Health Inequities in the Americas
papers.abstract: New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) within heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings across the Americas. This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement.

papers.title: Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action.
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infrastructure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical management, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases.

PEARLS Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action Nikhil Chakravarty 1,2, Vrithika Vaithi2, Arjit Vijey Jeyachandran2, Rakshiah Arunachalam2, Anne Zaiss2, Anna Bonazzi2, Mark Parcells3, Gustavo Garcia Jr.2, Arunachalam Ramaiah4*, Vaithilingaraja Arumugaswami 2,5,6,7* 1 Department of Medical Education,‌ California University of Science and Medicine, Colton, California, United States of America, 2 Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology,‌ University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 3 Department of Animal and Food Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, United States of America, 4 Georgia Public Health Laboratory, Georgia Department of Public Health, Decatur, Georgia, United States of America, 5 California NanoSystems Institute, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 6 Department of Bioengineering, Samueli School of Engineering, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 7 Eli & Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America * arunachalam.ramaiah@dph.ga.gov (AR); varumugaswami@mednet.ucla.edu (VA) Abstract In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infra­ structure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical manage­ ment, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases. A primer on the MV Hondius outbreak Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmis­ sion, underscoring its potential for outbreaks that extend beyond the traditional PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 2 / 11 rodent-to-human route. This significance became particularly clear in May 2026, when the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of several cases of severe respiratory illness aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries, as it transited the South Atlantic from Argentina. Only a few days later, at least 13 cases, including three deaths, were identified and/or ­laboratory-confirmed, including secondary cases among contacts of the index patient [1], as well as plane passengers in close proximity to confirmed cases on a flight to South Africa [2] and a repatriation flight from Tenerife [1–6]. Contact tracing and quarantine measures were coordinated through the WHO National IHR (International Health Regulations) Focal Points and implemented across several countries, includ­ ing the United Kingdom, South Africa, and the United States [2,3,7–10]. However, this outbreak is not the only recent notable case of hantaviral spread. In 2025, Betsy Arakawa, the wife of renowned actor Gene Hackman, passed away due to hantavirus infection in New Mexico, as did three people in Mammoth Lakes, California [11,12]. Hantavirus outbreaks highlight the challenge posed to public health agencies by neglected zoonotic pathogens—especially those that are ecologically complex, geographically distributed, understudied, and underfunded, yet capable of causing lethal outbreaks with little to no warning, thereby creating major public health concerns. As such, we aim to synthesize a brief primer on our current knowledge of hantaviruses and to propose areas for further research and development of emer­ gency preparedness and capacity building within existing public health infrastructure. What we know Epidemiologic history and global burden of Hantaviruses Old World (e.g., Hantaan [HTNV], Puumala [PUUV], Dobrava, and Seoul [SEOV] virus) and New World (e.g., Sin Nombre virus [SNV], ANDV) hantaviruses are primarily carried and spread asymptomatically in rodent reservoirs. The history of hantaviruses can be traced back to the Korean War in the 1950s, when over 3,000 troops stationed along the Hantaan River fell ill with a previously unknown virus, now known as HTNV [13] (Fig 1). The first recorded outbreak of hantaviruses in the United States occurred in 1993 in the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah [14,15]. Patients passed away from fever, myalgias, thrombocyto­ penia, and pulmonary edema with hypotensive shock, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the presence of SNV and its deer mouse reservoir. The spread of SNV was later associated with the 1991–1992 El Niño event, which caused warmer winters and increased spring rainfall, inciting a boom in the rodent population and promoting viral spread [14,15]. ANDV was first detected during a small outbreak in the Patagonia region of southern Argentina in 1995, with the first major outbreak of ANDV occurring in 2018–2019 in Epuyén, Argentina, where three distinct superspreader events occurred with no relation to inciting exposure to a rodent reservoir, confirming its ability to spread between humans [16]. The global burden associated with hantaviruses reflects two divergent clinical phenotypes. Old World viruses exhibit a case fatality rate (CFR) under 1% in settings with available vaccines and supportive care, whereas New World viruses carry an PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 3 / 11 estimated CFR of 30–60% [17,18]. In 2025, eight countries in the Americas reported 229 cases of hantaviral infections with a CFR of 25.7%. 1,885 cases were reported across Europe in 2023, and thousands of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) cases have been reported annually in East Asia [7].‌ Molecular virology and host-virus interactions Hantaviruses (class Bunyaviricetes, order Elliovirales, family Hantaviridae) [19–21] are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with a segmented genome (11–13 Kb) consisting of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, and are associated with an envelope protein containing viral glycoproteins [22,23]. In 2024, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) accepted a proposal to rename the class Ellioviricetes to Bunyaviricetes in RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) phylogeny and to split the order Bunyavirales into two orders, a broader classification based on observations of increased clustering into the two distinct orders Elliovirales (including families Fig 1. A visual history of major Hantavirus outbreaks. A schematic showing all major hantavirus outbreaks to date. Descriptive boxes are ­color-coded according to the type of hantavirus (Old World or New World) responsible, with the exception of the MV Hondius outbreak, which is high­ lighted red for emphasis. Additionally, regions with endemic hantaviruses are colored according to whether the endemic strain is an Old World (pink) or New World (blue) hantavirus. Image created in BioRender. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756.g001 PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 4 / 11 Hantaviridae and Peribunyaviridae) and Hareavirales (including families Arenaviridae, Nairoviridae, and Phenuiviridae) [20,21,24]. Hantaviruses can be dichotomized into two classes based on their geographic distribution: Old World viruses and New World viruses (Fig 1). The key distinction between these classes is the symptoms they cause: Old World viruses cause HFRS, and New World viruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS or HCPS) [17,25]. ANDV exhib­ its broad tropism, infecting multiple human cell types, including those of the heart, brain, and lungs, particularly lung epi­ thelial cells. It also induces cellular injury and inflammatory responses while suppressing lipid metabolic pathways in lung epithelial cells [26]. Though less common than pulmonary or cardiac manifestations, New World hantaviruses, particularly ANDV, have also been shown to induce neurological manifestations, such as confusion, meningoencephalitis, pituitary apoplexy, and, albeit rarely, seizures, myelitis, and peripheral neuropathy [27]. Gastrointestinal symptoms, including nau­ sea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, have also been observed in ANDV-infected patients, both preceding and in tandem with the onset of cardiovascular symptoms [28]. However, more investigation is needed to better understand the frequency of onset, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and the clinical significance of these symptoms. Since the 1950s [29,30], hantaviruses have been identified on every inhabited continent, with pathogenicity vary­ ing substantially across strains [22,23]. The differences in pathogenic mechanisms and disease outcomes among viral strains can be partly determined by viral-encoded factors, with several viral entry mechanisms elucidated in recent years. The viral M genome segment encodes glycoprotein precursors that are processed into Gn and Gc subunits, which form tetrameric complexes that help mediate cellular entry [31]. New World hantaviruses utilize protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to directly engage viral Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes and facilitate entry into vascular endothelial cells [32,33]. Recent investigations have elucidated the higher-order lattice architecture formed by Gn/Gc heterotetramers on the hantaviral surface, highlighting their role as the primarily necessary and sufficient proteins for viral attachment and entry [34,35]. Analysis of these surface spikes indicates that Gn/Gc complexes may serve as potential targets for antiviral immunothera­ peutic interventions, including neutralizing antibodies and structure-guided immunogens [36]. Upon viral entry and genome uncoating in the host-cell cytoplasm, the negative-strand genomes are transcribed into positive-strand mRNA by the viral RdRp. Similar to some other negative-sense RNA viruses, the hantaviral RdRp can also snatch 5’-capped mRNA fragments from host-cell transcripts, allowing the virus to use these sequences as primers for transcription and replication of the viral genome [37]. The nucleocapsid protein engages the viral RdRp and host ribo­ somes to selectively enhance translation of viral transcripts, while also interfering with protein kinase R (PKR) dimerization and remodeling of host proteostasis pathways, blunting cell-intrinsic antiviral defenses and promoting overall immune evasion [38,39]. Additionally, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to dampen early type I interferon (IFN) signaling in infected endothelial cells, thus sensitizing these cells to VEGF-mediated permeability [40,41]. This mechanism may underlie the pathogenesis of HFRS and HCPS. Hantaviruses can evade immune mechanisms by using structural and nonstructural proteins, such as NSs, NP, and Gn, to block RIG-I/MDA5-TBK1 signaling, antagonize IFN induction, and induce TUFM/LC3B-mediated mitophagy to degrade MAVS, respectively [42]. Of particular concern is the capacity of these viruses to evolve, driven by the error-prone RdRP, genetic reassortment events in the L segment, and hypervariable regions in the nucleocapsid protein encoded by the S segment [43,44]. Addi­ tionally, the lack of immunity in humans increases the capacity for viral transmission and virulence. This is especially con­ cerning given recent epidemiological trends in Argentina, which suggest that ANDV has a CFR of 34%, even higher than that of strains detected between 2019 and 2025 [45]. Phylogenetic analysis of the ANDV M-segment coding region against reference strains from NCBI revealed that the novel strain associated with the MV Hondius outbreak [46] shares 94.26% sequence identity with the ANDV reference sequence (NC_003467.2), indicating evolutionary divergence from the reference strain (Fig 2). Further comparison of this novel M-segment sequence against the NCBI Core Nucleotide Database identified closely related ANDV sequences isolated from human whole blood samples collected in Argentina (south variant) in 2018 (MN258191 and MN258192). These findings suggest that the lineage most closely related to this novel strain may have been circulating in human populations and/or reservoir hosts for nearly eight years, while gradually accumulating mutations PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 5 / 11 over time. Consistent with this inference, the novel strain’s M-coding region shows the highest sequence identity with the 2018 isolates (99.0% and 98.98%, respectively). Notably, the presence of 35 nucleotide mutations but only three amino acid substitutions, two in G1 (T193A and T516I) and one in G2 (A994T), within the glycoprotein-coding regions suggests strong purifying (negative) selection, preserving critical Gn and Gc functions. Overall, these findings indicate that the functional and transmission-relevant properties of ANDV are conserved across strains despite the accumulation of silent (synonymous) mutations, underscoring the importance of sustained genomic surveillance [47]. Human-to-human transmission of ANDV ANDV is unique in its capacity for human-to-human transmission, first suspected during the 1996 El Bolsón and Bariloche, Argentina, outbreaks and later confirmed at the molecular level soon after [48,49]. Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree con­ structed using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates (purple circles) for 38 M-segment sequences from the genus Orthohantavirus, including 35 species from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) RefSeq database, 2 species from GenBank (italicized), and 1 ANDV sequence (red font) obtained from a Swiss resident who had traveled on the MV Hondius cruise ship [46]. The clade containing the ANDV strain responsible for the current 2026 outbreak is highlighted in the pink box. Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.526, and the resulting alignment was used for ML phylogenetic tree construction in IQ-TREE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756.g002 PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 6 / 11 subsequently provided the most extensive documentation of this transmission route, as it was notable for three distinct superspreader events without any identifiable rodent exposure [50]. Although few additional ANDV outbreaks have been recorded, the MV Hondius outbreak provided further epidemiologic observations supporting this transmission route, including secondary cases among close contacts of symptomatic passengers [51]. It should be noted that, given the limited availability of outbreak-associated sequences and lack of continuous temporal sampling, we have avoided inferring direct or continuous viral transmission. Further investigation is needed to better establish the precise mechanisms, viral tropism for upper and lower respiratory tract airway epithelium, infectiousness duration, and full spectrum of transmission routes. Clinical management and therapeutics Management of hantaviral infections primarily consists of supportive care, with early detection and extracorporeal mem­ brane oxygenation (ECMO) in the cardiopulmonary phase remaining the most consistent determinants of survival [52,53]. Although Hantavax, an inactivated bivalent vaccine against HTNV, and a vaccine against SEOV are in active use across China and South Korea, no FDA-approved antivirals or vaccines are currently available for use in Western populations [53]. Several antiviral candidates have been investigated. Vandetanib demonstrated semi-prophylactic efficacy in Syr­ ian hamsters [54], while ribavirin, though promising in animal models, has generally not shown robust efficacy in human clinical trials [55–58]. PEARLS Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action Nikhil Chakravarty 1,2, Vrithika Vaithi2, Arjit Vijey Jeyachandran2, Rakshiah Arunachalam2, Anne Zaiss2, Anna Bonazzi2, Mark Parcells3, Gustavo Garcia Jr.2, Arunachalam Ramaiah4*, Vaithilingaraja Arumugaswami 2,5,6,7* 1 Department of Medical Education,‌ California University of Science and Medicine, Colton, California, United States of America, 2 Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology,‌ University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 3 Department of Animal and Food Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware, United States of America, 4 Georgia Public Health Laboratory, Georgia Department of Public Health, Decatur, Georgia, United States of America, 5 California NanoSystems Institute, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 6 Department of Bioengineering, Samueli School of Engineering, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America, 7 Eli & Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research, University of California, Los Angeles, California, United States of America * arunachalam.ramaiah@dph.ga.gov (AR); varumugaswami@mednet.ucla.edu (VA) Abstract In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infra­ structure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical manage­ ment, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases. A primer on the MV Hondius outbreak Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmis­ sion, underscoring its potential for outbreaks that extend beyond the traditional PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 2 / 11 rodent-to-human route. This significance became particularly clear in May 2026, when the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of several cases of severe respiratory illness aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries, as it transited the South Atlantic from Argentina. Only a few days later, at least 13 cases, including three deaths, were identified and/or ­laboratory-confirmed, including secondary cases among contacts of the index patient [1], as well as plane passengers in close proximity to confirmed cases on a flight to South Africa [2] and a repatriation flight from Tenerife [1–6]. Contact tracing and quarantine measures were coordinated through the WHO National IHR (International Health Regulations) Focal Points and implemented across several countries, includ­ ing the United Kingdom, South Africa, and the United States [2,3,7–10]. However, this outbreak is not the only recent notable case of hantaviral spread. In 2025, Betsy Arakawa, the wife of renowned actor Gene Hackman, passed away due to hantavirus infection in New Mexico, as did three people in Mammoth Lakes, California [11,12]. Hantavirus outbreaks highlight the challenge posed to public health agencies by neglected zoonotic pathogens—especially those that are ecologically complex, geographically distributed, understudied, and underfunded, yet capable of causing lethal outbreaks with little to no warning, thereby creating major public health concerns. As such, we aim to synthesize a brief primer on our current knowledge of hantaviruses and to propose areas for further research and development of emer­ gency preparedness and capacity building within existing public health infrastructure. What we know Epidemiologic history and global burden of Hantaviruses Old World (e.g., Hantaan [HTNV], Puumala [PUUV], Dobrava, and Seoul [SEOV] virus) and New World (e.g., Sin Nombre virus [SNV], ANDV) hantaviruses are primarily carried and spread asymptomatically in rodent reservoirs. The history of hantaviruses can be traced back to the Korean War in the 1950s, when over 3,000 troops stationed along the Hantaan River fell ill with a previously unknown virus, now known as HTNV [13] (Fig 1). The first recorded outbreak of hantaviruses in the United States occurred in 1993 in the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah [14,15]. Patients passed away from fever, myalgias, thrombocyto­ penia, and pulmonary edema with hypotensive shock, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the presence of SNV and its deer mouse reservoir. The spread of SNV was later associated with the 1991–1992 El Niño event, which caused warmer winters and increased spring rainfall, inciting a boom in the rodent population and promoting viral spread [14,15]. ANDV was first detected during a small outbreak in the Patagonia region of southern Argentina in 1995, with the first major outbreak of ANDV occurring in 2018–2019 in Epuyén, Argentina, where three distinct superspreader events occurred with no relation to inciting exposure to a rodent reservoir, confirming its ability to spread between humans [16]. The global burden associated with hantaviruses reflects two divergent clinical phenotypes. Old World viruses exhibit a case fatality rate (CFR) under 1% in settings with available vaccines and supportive care, whereas New World viruses carry an PLOS Pathogens | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 November 13, 2026 3 / 11 estimated CFR of 30–60% [17,18]. In 2025, eight countries in the Americas reported 229 cases of hantaviral infections with a CFR of 25.7%. 1,885 cases were reported across Europe in 2023, and thousands of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) cases have been reported annually in East Asia [7].‌ Molecular virology and host-virus interactions Hantaviruses (class Bunyaviricetes, order Elliovirales, family Hantaviridae) [19–21] are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with a segmented genome (11–13 Kb) consisting of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments,…

papers.title: Person-to-person transmission of Andes virus: a narrative review of current evidence and its clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses constitute a group of viruses responsible for emerging zoonotic diseases primarily transmitted by rodents. Andes virus (ANDV), endemic to South America, is unique among hantaviruses because of evidence supporting limited person-to-person transmission. The aim of this narrative review is to summarize current evidence regarding interpersonal transmission of ANDV and its clinical and epidemiological implications. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar including epidemiological studies, reviews, and experimental reports. Outbreaks described in Argentina and Chile, together with molecular studies and animal models, support the existence of person-to-person transmission in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly during the early stages of disease. Detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions provides biological plausibility for this phenomenon. The transmissibility of ANDV has relevant implications for patient isolation, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance in endemic regions.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic agents primarily transmitted from rodents to humans.
analysis.main_directions: Andes virus (ANDV) is unique among hantaviruses because limited person‑to‑person transmission has been reported, focusing the review on its transmission mechanisms and clinical impact.
analysis.current_state: Outbreak investigations in Argentina and Chile, supported by molecular studies and animal models, indicate that close, prolonged contact—especially early in disease—can lead to human‑to‑human spread.
analysis.gaps: While viral RNA has been detected in saliva and respiratory secretions, the frequency, risk factors, and precise routes of interpersonal transmission remain poorly quantified.

papers.title: Preventive and therapeutic strategies for hantavirus infection: a scoping review
papers.abstract: This project contains the protocol, search documentation, and supporting materials for a scoping review of preventive and therapeutic strategies for hantavirus infection. Purpose. Hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, and no antiviral agent or vaccine is licensed for global use. Research into countermeasures is scattered across rodent-control and public-health programmes, vaccine development, computational and experimental antiviral discovery, antibody and immunotherapeutic approaches, and intensive-care management. These bodies of work are rarely considered together, and no map of their collective extent exists. This review asks what evidence is available on preventive and therapeutic strategies for hantavirus infection, how it is distributed across preclinical, clinical and public-health settings, and where the gaps lie. Design. A scoping review conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, structured on a Population–Concept–Context framework with one primary and six secondary questions. Eligibility criteria were fixed before screening. No language restriction and no date restriction are applied. Sources include PubMed, Europe PMC, DOAJ, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO ICTRP, Chinese, Russian, Korean and Latin American regional databases, and citation searching of included records. A scoping design was chosen because the interventions concerned are not commensurable; no meta-analysis will be performed and critical appraisal of individual sources is not undertaken. Expected outputs. A PRISMA-ScR flow diagram, an evidence map cross-tabulating strategy category against evidence type, counts by hantavirus species, region and development stage, a narrative synthesis organised by question, and a gap analysis identifying translational barriers. Materials deposited here comprise the registered protocol, verbatim search strategies for every source, the charting form, and the screening and charting records. Reviewer arrangement. Screening is performed by a single human reviewer with machine-assisted pre-sorting. This does not constitute independent dual screening, and no inter-rater agreement statistic will be reported. This limitation is stated in the protocol. Funding. None.
