papers.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

papers.title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus– and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

papers.full_text: 1 Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory 1 epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses 2 Karine Badonnel 1,2, Thomas Cokelaer 3,4, Elodie Turc 5, Marc Monot 4,5, Jean Claude 3 Manuguerra 6, Myriam Ermonval 6#, and Giulia Gallo 7*#. 4 5 1 Université Paris-Saclay, UVSQ, INRAE, BREED, 78350, Jouy-en-Josas, France 6 2 Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d’Alfort, BREED, 94700, Maisons-Alfort, France 7 3 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Parasitologie Moléculaire et Signalisation, F-75015 Paris, 8 France 9 4 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Hub, F-75015 Paris, France 10 5 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Plate-forme Technologique Biomics, F-75015, Paris, France 11 6 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Environnement et Risques Infectieux, F-75015 Paris, France 12 7 The Pirbright Institute, Woking, United Kingdom 13 14 *Corresponding author: 15 Giulia.Gallo@pirbright.ac.uk (GG) 16 # Equally contributed to the work 17 18 19 Short tittle: response of bank vole cells to orthohantaviruses 20 21 Keywords: orthohantaviruses, Puumala virus, Tula virus, Prospect Hill virus, 22 transcriptomic analysis, bank vole cells, RNA-seq 23 24 25 Data availability 26 The RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 generated as part of this work were deposited to ENA 27 (accession E-MTAB-16656). 28 2 Abstract 29 Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause 30 diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. 31 While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, 32 hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune 33 response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the 34 modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments 35 in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, 36 are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better 37 understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between 38 organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural 39 hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends 40 on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at 41 different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA- 42 sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by 43 three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from 44 bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. 45 Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific 46 regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the 47 complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate 48 immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways. 49 50 Introduction 51 Orthohantaviruses (1) are found in small mammals, such as rodents, shrews, moles 52 and bats. Their long co-evolution with these globally distributed host species (2-4) 53 3 accounts for their presence in all continents (5). These viruses do not cause apparent 54 diseases in their natural hosts. Currently, only rodent-borne orthohantaviruses are 55 known to be pathogenic in humans, mainly through the inhalation of aerosols from 56 contaminated animal excreta. After entering the respiratory tract, orthohantaviruses 57 cross the pulmonary epithelial barrier and disseminate throughout the body by 58 infecting vascular endothelial cells and monocytes (6, 7). In humans, an exacerbated 59 immune response (8) leads to hemorrhagic fevers with renal syndromes (HFRS) and 60 nephropathia epidemica (NE) in the Old World (9), or to hantavirus cardio-pulmonary 61 syndromes (HCPS) in the Americas (10). The activation of innate immunity to 62 eliminate viruses, and the viral strategies to counteract it, vary depending on the 63 orthohantavirus species (11). Sustained interferon (IFN) activation may contribute to 64 inflammatory responses that influence viral pathogenicity (12). 65 We previously showed that the pathogenic Puumala virus (PUUV), the weakly 66 pathogenic Tula virus (TULV) and the non-pathogenic Prospect Hill virus (PHV), 67 differentially regulate IFN responses in human and rodent cells (13, 14). Myodes 68 glareolus (bank vole) is the natural host of PUUV, whereas TULV and PHV naturally 69 infect Microtus arvalis (common vole) and Microtus pensylvanicus (eastern meadow 70 vole), respectively. These orthohantaviruses exhibit different replication 71 characteristics in bank voles-derived cells. These differences correlate with cellular 72 restrictions acting at distinct stages of the viral cycle from entry to replication and viral 73 release (14). In human cells, type I and III IFNs and several IFN stimulated genes 74 (ISGs) are strongly activated by PUUV and PHV but not by TULV. In contrast, bank 75 vole cells display a delayed and weaker IFN response. 76 Despite advances in our understanding of the regulation of host responses in 77 rodents, the mechanisms leading to the differential outcomes of orthohantavirus 78 4 infection in their natural hosts remain poorly understood (15-18). To explore this 79 question, we compared gene expression profiles induced by PUUV, TULV and PHV. 80 Building on the opportunity that the recent availability of an updated Myodes 81 glareolus genome assembly in the NCBI database (GCF_902806735.1) provides, we 82 performed transcriptomic analysis by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of bank vole 83 epithelial cells derived from the kidneys (MyglaSWRecB) and the respiratory tract 84 (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) infected with these different orthohantaviruses. 85 Differential gene expression and pathway analyses revealed virus- and tissue- 86 specific regulatory programs that likely contribute to distinct infection outcomes and 87 host–virus interactions. 88 89 Material and methods 90 Cells and viruses 91 The three bank vole cells lines, MyglaSWRecB, MyglaSWTrach, MyglaAEC, 92 originated from kidney, tracheal and alveolar lung epithelium, respectively, and were 93 SV40 T antigen-immortalized (19). Cells were grown at 37°C with 5% CO2 in DMEM 94 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% of heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum 95 (Biosera). 96 Puumala Sotkamo viral strain (PUUV) and Prospect Hill viral strain (PHV) were 97 provided by Andreas Rang (Charité University, Berlin). Tula Moravia virus (TULV) 98 was obtained from Alexander Plyusnin (Helsinki University). Viral stocks were 99 propagated on Vero E6 cells as previously described (14). 100 RNA preparation, sequencing and transcriptomic analysis 101 RNA preparation from infected cells was performed as previously described (14). 102 Briefly, bank vole cells were infected with orthohantaviruses at a multiplicity of 103 5 infection (MOI) of 0.5. Total RNA was extracted 5 days post infection (dpi). After 104 washing with PBS, cells were treated with Trizol (Tri Reagent, Sigma Aldrich) and 105 chloroform. The aqueous phase containing the RNA was precipitated with 106 isopropanol and resuspended in distilled water. RNA concentration was measured 107 using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Four biological replicates 108 were generated for each condition: non-infected controls (NI) and cells infected with 109 PUUV, PHV or TULV orthohantaviruses. 110 Strand-specific single-end cDNA libraries were prepared from total RNA using 111 the Illumina Stranded mRNA prep, ligation preparation kit (Illumina) according to the 112 manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 113 platform. 114 RNA-seq analyses were performed using the Sequana framework, v0.14.1 (20). 115 Viral infection in samples was first verified using the Sequana mapper workflow to 116 detect specific viral RNA sequences. Transcriptomic analysis was conducted using 117 the Sequana RNA-seq pipeline (v0.15.2), implemented in Snakemake (21) and 118 available at https://github.com/sequana/sequana_RNA-seq, using default 119 parameters. Adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed with fastp v0.20.1 120 (22). Cleaned reads were aligned with STAR (23) against the Myodes glareolus 121 reference genome assembly GCA_902806735.1 and the Mus musculus reference 122 genome (GRCm38/mm10). Library strandedness was automatically inferred by the 123 pipeline, and gene-level counts were generated using FeatureCounts (package 124 Subread v2.0.1). Differential gene expression analysis was performed from the count 125 matrix using DESeq2 (v1.38.2) with R v4.2.1. Statistical significance was assessed 126 using Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values with a false discovery rate (FDR) 127 threshold of 0.05. 128 6 All third-party software dependencies were executed within containerized 129 environments provided through the Damona project (https://damona.readthedocs.io), 130 ensuring reproducibility. 131 Visualization of differentially expressed genes 132 Venn diagrams were drawn using the online Venny 2.1 program, an interactive tool 133 for comparing lists with Venn's diagrams (24) allowing the determination of the 134 number and identification of genes common or specific to a given situation. Volcano 135 plots and gene comparison representations were obtained using GraphPad Prism 11. 136 Heatmaps representations of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were 137 generated using the pheatmap function in the R program. This analysis was 138 performed for tracheal cells infected with PUUV, PHV, or TULV across the bank vole 139 and mouse reference genomes (BV and mm10). For each condition, only one entry 140 per gene was retained, prioritizing the lowest adjusted p-value (padj) and, in case of 141 ties, the largest absolute log2FoldChange. For the relative representation of genes 142 identified through the BV genome in comparison to the mm10 genome specifically in 143 infected tracheal cells, the six DEGs tables were merged by gene union, with missing 144 values replaced by zero. Genes with non-finite values (NA, NaN, Inf) or zero variance 145 across conditions were removed. Up and downregulated genes were defined based 146 on the sign of the mean log2FoldChange across the six conditions. Heatmaps were 147 generated using pheatmap in R, scaling values by gene (scale = "row"), clustering 148 columns using Euclidean distance and complete linkage, and annotating columns by 149 virus and genome. This approach enabled visualization of global expression profiles 150 and comparison of regulatory patterns across viruses and genomes. 151 Pathway enrichment 152 7 Functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was 153 performed using DAVID Bioinformatics Resources v6.8 154 (https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov/tools.jsp) (Database for Annotation, Visualization 155 and Integrated Discovery (25). Official gene symbols were submitted for annotation 156 clustering and enrichment analyses of Gene Ontology (GO) terms, KEGG and 157 Reactome pathways, and InterPro protein domains. The background dataset was set 158 to the entire Mus musculus genome, and Enriched terms were considered 159 statistically significant based on a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value < 0.05. 160 Data availability 161 The RNA-seq data set 1 was published in (14) with accession GSE198751. The 162 RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 were deposited to ENA (accession E-MTAB-16656). 163 164 Results 165 Quantitative gene regulation in kidney cells or in respiratory cells varies 166 depending on orthohantavirus species 167 To evaluate the effect of orthohantavirus infection on gene expression, different 168 epithelial bank vole (BV) cell lines derived from organs targeted by these viruses, 169 such as the respiratory tract (MyglaSWTrach and MyglaAEC#2) and the kidneys 170 (MyglaSWRecB), were infected at a MOI of 0.5 with PUUV, TULV or PHV and their 171 RNAs extracted five days post infection (5 dpi). At this time point, the viral replication 172 of PUUV and PHV is clearly detectable and constitutes a suitable basis for the 173 quantitative and qualitative characterization of gene expression by RNA-seq, as 174 previously described (14). The experimental approach is schematized in Figure 1. 175 The RNA-seq generated a similar number of reads (20-30 million) to each sample 176 and these samples are clustered according to infection status distinguishing 177 8 uninfected and infected conditions (Fig. SD1). The number of identified genes 178 significantly upregulated and downregulated (FC>2 and <-2, p-value <0.05), varied 179 according to the virus and cell types (Table 1). Venn diagrams illustrate, in addition to 180 the number of genes, the percentage of genes specific or common to different 181 situations. Since few genes were upregulated upon orthohantavirus infection of 182 pulmonary alveolar MyglaAEC#2 cells (Table 1), they were not included in Venn 183 diagrams and volcano plot representations. Around 70% of differentially expressed 184 genes (DEGs), were upregulated and 30% were downregulated. However, more 185 genes appeared differentially expressed (DE) in the infected tracheal cells than in the 186 kidney cells, both with PUUV (308 vs 66, Fig. 2A) and PHV (545 vs 254, Fig. 2B). 187 Strikingly, few DEGs were common to these two cell lines upon PUUV infection 188 (1.1%) or PHV infection (8.1%). In the case of TULV (Table 1) very few genes were 189 DE in MyglaSWRecB compared to what is seen in MyglaSWTrach (4 vs 509). 190 While TULV did not induce significant gene regulation in the kidney cell line, 191 PUUV and PHV did (Fig. 3A). Indeed, in MyglaSWRecB cells, 37 of 66 genes (56%) 192 were specifically regulated by PUUV, and 226 of 254 genes (88.9.%) by PHV. This 193 represented 12.5% and 76.6% of the total identified genes for PUUV and PHV 194 respectively, when only 9.5% of genes were common to PUUV- and PHV-infected 195 cells. In the tracheal cells, MyglaSWTrach, the situation was quite different (Fig 3B). 196 Many more genes were DE upon infection with the nonpathogenic orthohantaviruses, 197 PHV (545) and TULV (509), than with PUUV (308). Among these genes, only 10.5% 198 were specific to PUUV infection, 21.6% to PHV infection and 15.4% to TULV 199 infection. Interestingly, in this cell line, a higher proportion of DEGs was shared 200 following infection with all three orthohantaviruses (21.2%) or with the non- 201 pathogenic heterologous orthohantaviruses PHV and TULV (23.7%). In contrast, 202 9 fewer genes were common to PUUV and PHV or PUUV and TULV (3.1% and 4;6% 203 respectively). Although the volcano plots show gene expression levels 204 (log2FoldChange) and their significance (-log10_adjusted p-value), it should be noted 205 that more genes were upregulated than downregulated in each situation (Fig. 3C). 206 Due to the limited information available for the bank vole genome, our previous 207 work identified DEGs in infected renal cells from the mouse database (mm10). 208 Therefore, the RNA-seq data generated in the present study were also analyzed 209 against this mouse database. The percentage of DEGs found in infected tracheal 210 (Fig. SD2A) or renal (Fig. SD3A) cells, specific or common to different viruses was 211 similar, whether using the bank vole or the mouse reference genome. However, it is 212 worth noting that for PUUV, PHV and TULV, only about 20% of the identified genes in 213 MyglaSWTrach cells were found with the two genomes (Fig. SD2B), highlighting the 214 importance of combining the two analyses. The same observation was made for the 215 renal cells (Fig. SD3B), where an even smaller percentage of genes appeared 216 common to the two databases. This result should nevertheless be viewed with 217 caution due to the small number of DEGs identified after PUUV infection of 218 MyglaSWRecB cells. Therefore, all the annotated genes found in the mouse and vole 219 reference genomes were compiled into a single list of identification (Table 2 and 220 Table SD). It should also be noted that many genes annotated as genomic loci (Loc 221 genes) have orthologues in the mouse or human genome. This is for instance the 222 case for 25, 54 and 42 Loc genes (FC>4 and <-4), for PUUV, PHV and TULV 223 respectively in tracheal infected cells, and for 7 and 72 genes, for PUUV and PHV in 224 renal infected cells. The putative corresponding names of these identified sequences 225 have been added to the tables (in blue) and when several sequences referred to a 226 similar orthologue, only the one with the highest FC value was retained. 227 10 Innate immune responses are activated by orthohantaviruses in kidney and 228 respiratory epithelial cells from bank vole 229 We compared the DEGs identified in the renal and the tracheal cell lines infected with 230 the different orthohantaviruses, PUUV, PHV, TULV, using the bank vole and the 231 mouse reference genomes (Table 2). The transcripts regulated by one or more 232 viruses in different BV cell lines (Fig. 4A) were mainly involved in antiviral defense as 233 expected following the recognition of RNA viruses by Toll-, Nod- or Rig1-like 234 receptors (TLR, NLR, RLR) upstream of innate immune responses (12). Only two 235 genes were significantly activated by PUUV (FC>2) in both MyglaSWTrach and 236 MyglaSWRecB cell lines; Ddx60, a helicase promoting RLR signaling, and the IFN- 237 inducible gene Ifit1, known to inhibit viral replication (26). These two genes were also 238 upregulated by PHV in these two BV cell lines. It is remarkable that only a few ISGs 239 were slightly upregulated by PUUV, the orthohantavirus specifically transmitted by 240 bank voles, as compared with the much stronger induction observed following 241 infection with the heterologous orthohantavirus PHV. full_text_sections.full_text: 1 Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory 1 epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses 2 Karine Badonnel 1,2, Thomas Cokelaer 3,4, Elodie Turc 5, Marc Monot 4,5, Jean Claude 3 Manuguerra 6, Myriam Ermonval 6#, and Giulia Gallo 7*#. 4 5 1 Université Paris-Saclay, UVSQ, INRAE, BREED, 78350, Jouy-en-Josas, France 6 2 Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d’Alfort, BREED, 94700, Maisons-Alfort, France 7 3 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Parasitologie Moléculaire et Signalisation, F-75015 Paris, 8 France 9 4 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Bioinformatics and Biostatistics Hub, F-75015 Paris, France 10 5 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Plate-forme Technologique Biomics, F-75015, Paris, France 11 6 Institut Pasteur, Université Paris Cité, Environnement et Risques Infectieux, F-75015 Paris, France 12 7 The Pirbright Institute, Woking, United Kingdom 13 14 *Corresponding author: 15 Giulia.Gallo@pirbright.ac.uk (GG) 16 # Equally contributed to the work 17 18 19 Short tittle: response of bank vole cells to orthohantaviruses 20 21 Keywords: orthohantaviruses, Puumala virus, Tula virus, Prospect Hill virus, 22 transcriptomic analysis, bank vole cells, RNA-seq 23 24 25 Data availability 26 The RNA-seq data set 2 and 3 generated as part of this work were deposited to ENA 27 (accession E-MTAB-16656). 28 2 Abstract 29 Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause 30 diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. 31 While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, 32 hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune 33 response. papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

papers.full_text: Frontiers in Veterinary Science 01 frontiersin.org Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness Muhammad Inam 1* and Hamid Khan 2* 1School of Medicine, Qilu Institute of Technology, Jinan, China, 2Institute of Brain Science and Brain- Inspired Research, Shandong First Medical University and Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences, Jinan, China Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on under­ standing reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they inter­ sect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is estab­ lished. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, work­ load, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively. KEYWORDS Andes virus, hantavirus, occupational exposure, One Health, orthohantavirus, preparedness, rodent reservoir, surveillance 1 Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, three-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses in the family Hantaviridae, order Elliovirales. Rodent-associated orthohantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across much of Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syn­ drome (HCPS) in the Americas (1–3). The transmission cycle brings clinical care into contact with wildlife ecology, occupational health, veterinary practice, and laboratory biosafety. The defining One Health feature of hantavirus epidemiology is that the maintenance cycle operates entirely outside health services. Reservoir abundance and species composition, food availability, rainfall, temperature, land use, agricultural practice, housing quality, waste man­ agement and human behavior together determine whether infected animals contaminate spaces that people use (1, 4, 5). Humans are usually exposed by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or through direct contact with contaminated material. TYPE Review PUBLISHED 30 October 2026 DOI 10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Bernard J. Phiri, Ministry for Primary Industries, New Zealand REVIEWED BY Arif Nur Muhammad Ansori, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Indonesia Yunhui Xiang, Sichuan International Travel and Healthcare Center (Chengdu Customs District Port Clinic), China *CORRESPONDENCE Muhammad Inam 2022390020@gzhmu.edu.cn Hamid Khan hamidkhan193@gmail.com RECEIVED 08 August 2026 REVISED 02 October 2026 ACCEPTED 08 October 2026 PUBLISHED 30 October 2026 CITATION Inam M and Khan H (2026) Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness. Front. Vet. Sci. 13:1962397. doi: 10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 COPYRIGHT © 2026 Inam and Khan. This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). The use, distribution or reproduction in other forums is permitted, provided the original author(s) and the copyright owner(s) are credited and that the original publication in this journal is cited, in accordance with accepted academic practice. No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 02 frontiersin.org Prevention therefore depends on recognizing and modifying ecologi­ cal and occupational interfaces before a patient reaches clinical care. A systematic review of land cover and land use found agricultural land use positively associated with human infection risk in China and Brazil and forest cover positively associated with incidence in Europe, while associations with built-up areas differed in direction between studies (6). Surveillance coverage differs markedly between regions. Some countries have paired human case reporting with reservoir monitor­ ing for decades, while others rely on a few serosurveys or small wild­ life studies, and some have no structured reservoir data at all (7–9). This makes country comparisons difficult: few reported cases may indicate genuinely low transmission, limited diagnostic access, missed cases, or simply insufficient surveillance. A meta-analysis of small mammals across Southeast Asia estimated a pooled hantavirus preva­ lence of 6.07% among 11,806 animals, with the highest estimates in Indonesia and Singapore, in a region where human diagnostic recog­ nition remains limited (8). Work in Cambodia detected orthohanta­ virus RNA in 3.3% of 750 rodents and IgG seropositivity in 10.0% of people sampled at the same sites, with the highest rodent infection rates at urban rather than rural interfaces (9). Attention to these questions has been renewed by the 2026 multi- country Andes virus (ANDV) event linked to an expedition cruise ship, which produced 13 cases and three deaths, contact tracing across more than 30 countries and territories, and a sequence of international notifications before it was declared over in July 2026 (10). The event does not indicate that hantaviruses have become more widespread. It illustrates how a rare zoonosis moving through a mobile and medi­ cally constrained exposure network can rapidly test diagnostic referral pathways and risk communication in settings without endemic transmission. Recent field surveys, systematic reviews, and outbreak reports from 2024 to 2026 have expanded the evidence base on host range, land use, geographic surveillance gaps, and international response (6–10). Yet descriptive One Health reviews seldom specify how a low- capacity setting should move from baseline sampling to an investiga­ tion, or when an enhanced response can safely be reduced (11, 12). This review brings together reservoir biology, exposure, diagnostics, and surveillance to propose explicit, locally adaptable decision steps. The framework is an operational hypothesis, not an established standard. 2 Scope and evidence framing 2.1 Review design and information sources This structured narrative review brings together evidence on hantavirus reservoirs, human exposure, diagnosis, and One Health surveillance. We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. The purpose was to examine evidence relevant to practical surveillance decisions across different epidemiological settings. 2.2 Evidence eligibility and selection Studies were retained when they directly informed one or more areas addressed in this review, including reservoir ecology and host relationships, animal-to-human exposure, human epidemiology, vet­ erinary or occupational risk, diagnostic and genomic methods, envi­ ronmental and land-use influences, surveillance, and preparedness. For specific epidemiological or laboratory statements, we relied mainly on peer-reviewed primary research; systematic and narrative reviews were used to place individual findings in a broader context. We also used guidance and outbreak reports from WHO, CDC, ECDC, and similar public or animal health agencies when these sources provided operational information not available in journal articles. We generally excluded papers devoted only to treatment or molecular mechanisms with no clear relevance to exposure or One Health surveillance, duplicate or substantially overlapping reports, studies with too little methodological detail to interpret, conference abstracts, and non-authoritative web sources. 2.3 Evidence synthesis and framework development Priority was given to primary epidemiological, virological, reser­ voir, genomic, diagnostic and occupational studies, with systematic reviews and authoritative narrative reviews used for broader contex­ tual statements. The synthesis was organized around five recurring questions: which animals maintain infection, where human exposure occurs, which populations are most exposed, how infection can be reliably detected, and how animal, human and environmental infor­ mation can be combined into surveillance and prevention (11, 13, 14). Because the literature considered differed substantially in study design, host species, geographic setting, diagnostic method, surveil­ lance intensity, and reported outcomes, quantitative pooling was not considered appropriate. Findings were synthesized narratively across epidemiological settings, with particular attention to consistency, directness of evidence, methodological clarity, and operational rele­ vance. Greater interpretive weight was given to longitudinal surveil­ lance, well-characterized reservoir studies, linked human-animal investigations, molecularly confirmed outbreaks, and studies with clearly described sampling and diagnostic methods. The tiered sur­ veillance framework was developed from recurring operational needs identified across these evidence domains and should be interpreted as an evidence-informed proposal rather than a formally validated guideline. We considered five dimensions when interpreting a study: rele­ vance to the question; reliable identification of the host and infection; a clear sampling denominator, time frame, and assay; a longitudinal or linked human-animal design when needed to support an inference; and agreement or disagreement with findings from other settings. A serological result without supporting exposure or molecular data was not taken as evidence of current transmission. These considerations informed the narrative synthesis rather than a formal quality score. Table 1 illustrates the kinds of evidence and methodological con­ straints that shaped the proposed surveillance framework. Inam and Khan  10.3389/fvets.2026.1962397 Frontiers in Veterinary Science 03 frontiersin.org 2.4 Terminology and interpretive principles Terminology is used deliberately throughout. Hantavirus refers to the group, while orthohantavirus is used where taxonomic precision is required. We distinguish reservoir hosts, in which infection is per­ sistent and largely asymptomatic, from incidental hosts, and we dis­ tinguish serological evidence of past exposure from molecular detection of viral RNA, reservoir infection from human exposure, and human exposure from confirmed disease. Antibody detection in a rodent or a person is not by itself evidence of current transmission, and a positive rodent does not establish human disease risk in the absence of a plausible exposure pathway. One interpretive principle applies throughout: absence of pub­ lished surveillance is not equivalent to absence of infection. Evidence- sparse settings are therefore discussed in terms of surveillance gaps and preparedness needs rather than assumed local transmission or assumed local safety. The distinction matters particularly for neglected zoonoses, where diagnostic capacity and small-mammal sampling tend to be concentrated in a small number of research centers. 3 Hantavirus biology and disease spectrum The genome comprises small (S), medium (M) and large (L) seg­ ments encoding the nucleocapsid protein, the Gn/Gc glycoprotein precursor and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively (15). Genetic diversity arises through mutation, reassortment, pro­ longed host association and occasional host-switching events (16, 17). TABLE 1 Selected evidence informing the design of integrated hantavirus surveillance. A survey of small-mammal communi­ ties in New Mexico detected Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in 27% of ani­ mals sampled and recovered infectious virus from tissues and feces of species other than the recognized primary reservoir, indicating that alternative and previously unrecognized reservoirs can both maintain and shed the virus (18). full_text_sections.full_text: Frontiers in Veterinary Science 01 frontiersin.org Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness Muhammad Inam 1* and Hamid Khan 2* 1School of Medicine, Qilu Institute of Technology, Jinan, China, 2Institute of Brain Science and Brain- Inspired Research, Shandong First Medical University and Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences, Jinan, China Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on under­ standing reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they inter­ sect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is estab­ lished. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, work­ load, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively. KEYWORDS Andes virus, hantavirus, occupational exposure, One Health, orthohantavirus, preparedness, rodent reservoir, surveillance 1 Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, three-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses in the family Hantaviridae, order Elliovirales. Rodent-associated orthohantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) across much of Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syn­ drome (HCPS) in the Americas (1–3). The transmission cycle brings clinical care into contact with wildlife ecology, occupational health, veterinary practice, and laboratory biosafety. The defining One Health feature of hantavirus epidemiology is that the maintenance cycle operates entirely outside health services. Reservoir abundance and species composition, food availability, rainfall, temperature, land use, agricultural practice, housing quality, waste man­ agement and human behavior together determine whether infected animals contaminate spaces that people use (1, 4, 5). Humans are usually exposed by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, feces, or saliva, or through direct contact with contaminated material. A systematic review of land cover and land use found agricultural land use positively associated with human infection risk in China and Brazil and forest cover positively associated with incidence in Europe, while associations with built-up areas differed in direction between studies (6). Surveillance coverage differs markedly between regions. Some countries have paired human case reporting with reservoir monitor­ ing for decades, while others rely on a few serosurveys or small wild­ life studies, and some have no structured reservoir data at all (7–9). This makes country comparisons difficult: few reported cases may indicate genuinely low transmission, limited diagnostic access, missed cases, or simply insufficient surveillance. A meta-analysis of small mammals across Southeast Asia estimated a pooled hantavirus preva­ lence of 6.07% among 11,806 animals, with the highest estimates in Indonesia and Singapore, in a region where human diagnostic recog­ nition remains limited (8). Work in Cambodia detected orthohanta­ virus RNA in 3.3% of 750 rodents and IgG seropositivity in 10.0% of people sampled at the same sites, with the highest rodent infection rates at urban rather than rural interfaces (9). Attention to these questions has been renewed by the 2026 multi- country Andes virus (ANDV) event linked to an expedition cruise ship, which produced 13 cases and three deaths, contact tracing across more than 30 countries and territories, and a sequence of international notifications before it was declared over in July 2026 (10). The event does not indicate that hantaviruses have become more widespread. It illustrates how a rare zoonosis moving through a mobile and medi­ cally constrained exposure network can rapidly test diagnostic referral pathways and risk communication in settings without endemic transmission. Recent field surveys, systematic reviews, and outbreak reports from 2024 to 2026 have expanded the evidence base on host range, land use, geographic surveillance gaps, and international response (6–10). Yet descriptive One Health reviews seldom specify how a low- capacity setting should move from baseline sampling to an investiga­ tion, or when an enhanced response can safely be reduced (11, 12). This review brings together reservoir biology, exposure, diagnostics, and surveillance to propose explicit, locally adaptable decision steps. The framework is an operational hypothesis, not an established standard. 2 Scope and evidence framing 2.1 Review design and information sources This structured narrative review brings together evidence on hantavirus reservoirs, human exposure, diagnosis, and One Health surveillance. We searched literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar, reference lists, and reports from public health agencies. The searches were updated in August 2026. Studies published from 2000 onward received particular attention, while earlier work was retained when it remained founda­ tional to the biology or clinical picture. Searches combined “hantavirus” or “orthohantavirus” with terms for five related domains: reservoir hosts and ecology; occupa­ tional, veterinary and household exposure; serology, molecular diag­ nosis and genomic epidemiology; surveillance, land use and climate; and Andes virus outbreaks and contact management. Terms and combinations were adapted to each database and refined as the review developed. papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective.
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges. full_text_sections.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. Methods Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. Results A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. Conclusions The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 分子诊断与病毒RNA动力学,使用仅限研究用途的RT-PCR检测:西班牙一家三级医院的经验。

analysis_zh.background: 该研究针对西班牙一次输入性暴发期间对安第斯病毒(ANDV)可靠诊断的需求,评估了一种仅供研究使用的RT‐PCR检测方法。
analysis_zh.methods: 对14名遣返人员进行全血和血清筛查;对两例确诊病例进行前瞻性随访,每72小时采集一次全血、血清、口咽拭子、尿液和直肠拭子。标本在BSL‐3实验室灭活,RNA自动提取,并使用RealStar® 汉坦病毒‐HPS RT‐PCR检测,同时使用汉坦病毒特异性参考RT‐PCR进行比对。

analysis_zh.limitations: 本研究为描述性,未建立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性,仍需进一步的分析和临床研究;本分析仅基于摘要。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.
